newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile stumbles in plans to privatize water.
newsitem.headline: Chile stumbles in plans to privatize water.

text.p: Chile's ambitious plan to privatize all its state-owned water works has run into unexpected political trouble after leaders of President Eduardo Frei's own party said they opposed the plan.

After a year of languishing in Congress, the project took a body blow when the Christian Democratic Party's ruling council repudiated the plan on grounds it granted too many concessions to potential buyers.
The decision means privatization in its current form is unlikely to get the green light from Congress.

Supporters say the plan, part of Frei's grand strategy to sell off key infrastructure including ports, airports and some highway projects, will be revised and refloated. But officials at companies that have already gone on record as potential bidders have given up hope for next year and some see the process on hold indefinitely, news reports said.

"We are at a critical moment in the bill's passage through Congress," said deputy Ignacio Walker, a Christian Democrat and a key supporter. "But I would consider (the council's decision) as a wake-up call, not the end of the project," he told Reuters.
The project to sell off controlling stakes in water works, proposed by Frei in May 1995, hit trouble when the Senate rewrote the bill to make it more attractive to potential buyers.
Controlled by the right-wing opposition, the Senate allowed private concerns to buy 100 percent of the firms and weakened regulations on them.

The regulations were aimed at guaranteeing basic service conditions, preventing monopolies by ensuring there would be at least four or five private operators in the whole country, and mandating a certain amount of investment.
Under the original bill, privatization would start with water works in the Valparaiso area and the southern Tenth Region and then be gradually extended to the rest of the country.

Severe drought in central Chile has also weakened public support for the plan. Customers of a private water works in Santiago's rich eastern suburbs, Lo Castillo SA, have endured water rationing for weeks while customers of the state-controlled company, Emos, have had their taps flowing.

The difference was that while Lo Castillo was returning money to its stockholders and investing little, Emos was busily sinking new wells and investing in new equipment, a series of news investigations have shown.
"Emos is perceived as an example of a well-run public company and people don't see the point in privatizing it," said a government official closely involved in the issue.
Lo Castillo's new owner Enersis SA, which bought the company last month, has promised a $200 million investment plan for the pilloried company over the next two years.
That's nothing compared with what bidders for the whole Chilean water works system would have to invest -- some $2 billion between now and 2000, according to Frei's plan.
Interested companies include Enersis, Chilgener SA and Chilquinta, as well as foreign firms Thames Water Plc, Compagnie Generale des Eaux and Aguas de Barcelona, news reports have said.
Not waiting for Chile to get its act together, Enersis may bid for Argentine water works Obras Sanitarias Mendoza SA, slated for privatization, newspaper Estrategia reported.
